reference.title: Band Reverse fly
reference.listing: Video (movement reference only; the page could not be fetched from the authoring environment, so the data sheet was not read)

breathing.pattern: Breathe out as the arms sweep out, breathe in as they come back together.
breathing.cadence: About 1 s out, short squeeze, about 2 s back

prescription.load: Band tension is user-chosen: light enough to reach the T with straight arms
prescription.progression: More reps, a longer squeeze, a step further from the rack or a stronger band

cues.text: Loop the band round a rack upright at shoulder height. Face it, feet hip width, a strand in each hand, palms facing each other, arms straight in front at shoulder height.
Breathe out and sweep the straight arms out and back, leading with the backs of the hands.
Stop with the arms in a T, in line with the shoulders; squeeze the shoulder blades together, shoulders down, ribs down.
Breathe in and bring the arms back in front slowly, keeping the band tight.
Brief pause in front, then repeat.

mistakes.mistake: Bending the elbows to finish (turning it into a row)
mistakes.fix: Keep the arms long; use a lighter band or step closer.
Keep the shoulders down away from the ears.

mistakes.mistake: Swinging the arms back past the shoulders and arching the back
mistakes.fix: Stop at the T, ribs down.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the band pull the arms forward fast

kinematics.norm: From arms straight in front to a T in line with the shoulders (clinical opinion)
About shoulder height, near 90 degrees of elevation; prone horizontal abduction was tested at about 100 degrees of abduction (Reinold 2007)
Retract (squeeze together) at the end; in prone retraction exercises the middle trapezius reached up to about 77% of maximal activity with the arms raised (Oyama 2010)
Neutral (palms facing each other) gave more posterior deltoid activity than a pronated grip on a reverse fly (Schoenfeld 2013)

Anchored in front, the band pulls the arms forward through the whole arc, and its tension rises as it stretches; at matched effort elastic tubing and dumbbells gave similar activity in shoulder exercises (Andersen 2010)
About 1 s apart, 2 s back (clinical opinion)

sources.title: GymVisual #13781, Band Reverse fly, video (movement reference)
Reinold et al. 2007, electromyographic analysis of the supraspinatus and deltoid muscles during 3 common rehabilitation exercises (J Athl Train 42(4):464-469)
Oyama, Myers, Wassinger and Lephart 2010, three-dimensional scapular and clavicular kinematics and scapular muscle activity during retraction exercises (J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 40(3):169-179)
Schoenfeld et al. 2013, effect of hand position on EMG activity of the posterior shoulder musculature during a horizontal abduction exercise (J Strength Cond Res 27(10):2644-2649)

Andersen, Andersen, Mortensen, Poulsen, Bjornlund and Zebis 2010, muscle activation and perceived loading during rehabilitation exercises: comparison of dumbbells and elastic resistance (Phys Ther 90(4):538-549)

cautions: Stop if sharp pain, a pinching feeling in the shoulder, numbness or tingling occurs.
Check the band for nicks or tears and loop it securely round the upright; a band that slips or snaps can hit the face.
Band tension is user-chosen: pick one you can sweep to a T with straight arms.
Muscle glow colours and activation curves are illustrative, not measured EMG.
modify: Shoulder discomfort: sweep a little lower, at chest height, and stop short of the T.
Cannot keep the arms straight: soften the elbows a little more or use a lighter band.
regressions: Lighter band or a step closer to the rack.
Partial range, stopping with the hands in line with the shoulders.
progressions: Stronger band or a step further back.

muscleNotes.post_deltoid_r: Prime mover: horizontal abduction of the straight arm against the band. Prone horizontal abduction reached about 87% MVIC in the posterior deltoid (Reinold 2007); a neutral grip gave more posterior deltoid activity than a pronated grip on a reverse fly (Schoenfeld 2013).
muscleNotes.post_deltoid_l: Prime mover: horizontal abduction of the straight arm against the band. Prone horizontal abduction reached about 87% MVIC in the posterior deltoid (Reinold 2007); a neutral grip gave more posterior deltoid activity than a pronated grip on a reverse fly (Schoenfeld 2013).
muscleNotes.rhomboids_midtrap_r: Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the end. In prone retraction exercises the middle trapezius reached up to about 77% of maximal activity with the arms raised (Oyama 2010); the rhomboids could not be measured with surface EMG.
muscleNotes.rhomboids_midtrap_l: Squeeze the shoulder blades together at the end. In prone retraction exercises the middle trapezius reached up to about 77% of maximal activity with the arms raised (Oyama 2010); the rhomboids could not be measured with surface EMG.
muscleNotes.infraspinatus_r: External rotator that works with the posterior deltoid; higher with a neutral grip (Schoenfeld 2013).
muscleNotes.infraspinatus_l: External rotator that works with the posterior deltoid; higher with a neutral grip (Schoenfeld 2013).
muscleNotes.lat_deltoid_r: Holds the arm up at shoulder height; prone horizontal abduction also gave about 63% MVIC in the middle deltoid (Reinold 2007).
muscleNotes.lat_deltoid_l: Holds the arm up at shoulder height; prone horizontal abduction also gave about 63% MVIC in the middle deltoid (Reinold 2007).
muscleNotes.upper_traps_r: Steadies the shoulder blade; shrugging shifts work here.
muscleNotes.upper_traps_l: Steadies the shoulder blade; shrugging shifts work here.
muscleNotes.core: Keeps the ribs down so the low back does not arch.

guides.label: Straight arm sweeps out to a T at shoulder height
